::: {.question-box}
Can I reproduce a published result from the original data, and do I understand every step?
:::

## Why reproduce papers?

Reading a methods section is easy. Getting the same numbers from the raw data is where the
real learning happens. Each lab follows the same pattern: **get the data → rebuild the analysis →
compare with the paper → write down what was hard**.

::: {.card-grid}
::: {.cute-card}
[🐧]{.icon .bg-sky}

### Palmer penguins

Gorman et al. (2014): body measurements and sexual dimorphism in Antarctic penguins. A warm-up in tidy data and plotting.
:::
::: {.cute-card}
[🥔]{.icon .bg-butter}

### Potato GWAS

Linking SNPs to traits: kinship, population structure and Manhattan plots.
:::
::: {.cute-card}
[🧪]{.icon .bg-blush}

### RNA-seq (airway)

Differential expression on the classic airway dataset, from counts to volcano plot.
:::
::: {.cute-card}
[📚]{.icon .bg-lavender}

### Disease text mining

Pulling disease mentions out of the literature and seeing what patterns appear.
:::
:::

## Beyond the labs

I'm also working through study projects in **variant calling, proteomics, metabolomics,
microbiome analysis, multi-omics integration** and **wheat text mining**, all tracked on my
[study hub](../rush-hub/).

## What I learned

::: {.learned}
- Published methods often leave out small but important choices. Reproducing them shows you where.
- Matching a paper's numbers exactly is hard, and explaining the gaps is a skill in itself.
:::
